taxonomy.subtopic: Increased fixed outflow resistance and the left ventricular pressure-volume loop

questions.stem_html: A 76-year-old man has progressive exertional chest pressure and two episodes of near-syncope. Examination shows a late-peaking systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotid arteries. The accompanying pressure-volume diagram compares his left ventricle with a normal ventricle. Which change best explains the altered loop?

options.text_html: An increase in left ventricular afterload that raises end-systolic volume and narrows stroke volume
A decrease in ventricular afterload that lowers end-systolic volume and widens stroke volume
Acute volume overload that abolishes isovolumetric contraction
A decrease in myocardial oxygen demand caused by reduced systolic wall stress
An increase in ventricular compliance that lowers end-diastolic pressure at every volume

questions.explanation_html: A stenotic aortic valve creates fixed resistance to ejection. The left ventricle must generate higher systolic pressure, so effective afterload rises. With contractility and preload otherwise unchanged, more blood remains at end systole and stroke volume falls, producing a taller, narrower loop. Chronic pressure overload also promotes concentric hypertrophy and increases oxygen demand.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Reduced afterload facilitates ejection, decreases end-systolic volume, and increases stroke volume.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Aortic stenosis commonly causes concentric hypertrophy and impaired relaxation rather than increased compliance.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Isovolumetric contraction remains present; loss of an isovolumetric phase is characteristic of regurgitation.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: High systolic pressure and hypertrophy increase myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.educational_objective: Fixed aortic outflow obstruction increases left ventricular afterload, systolic pressure, and end-systolic volume while reducing stroke volume.

media.alt_text: Pressure-volume loops comparing a normal ventricle with a taller, narrower loop caused by aortic stenosis.
